opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most exciting areas right now, and the way I see it, they're really complementary rather than competing approaches.

Supervised fine-tuning is great for getting the model into the right neighborhood. If you have good demonstrations of tool use, how to format a function call, when to call a tool versus answer directly, how to parse the result and continue, SFT teaches the model the basic grammar of that behavior very efficiently. It's sample-efficient, it's stable, and it gives you a strong starting point. The problem is that SFT only teaches the model to imitate. It doesn't really learn *why* a particular sequence of tool calls was good, and it can struggle when it ends up in states that weren't in the demonstration data. Small errors compound over a multi-step trajectory.

That's where RL comes in. Tool calling is actually a really natural fit for reinforcement learning, because in a lot of cases you have verifiable outcomes. Did the code execute? Did the API return the right thing? Did the final answer match? You can get a reward signal without needing a human to label every step. So once the model has learned the basic format through SFT, RL lets it explore and discover strategies that might not be in your demonstrations: recovering from a failed call, choosing a more efficient sequence of tools, knowing when to stop.

The recipe that seems to work well in practice is SFT first as a warm start, maybe on a relatively small but high-quality dataset, and then RL on top of that with outcome-based rewards. If you skip the SFT step and go straight to RL, the model often doesn't produce valid tool calls often enough to get any reward signal, so exploration is really inefficient. And if you only do SFT, you plateau at roughly the quality of your data.

There are also interesting loops you can build between the two. You can use RL or even just rejection sampling to generate successful trajectories, filter for the ones that actually worked, and feed those back in as SFT data. That kind of iterative self-improvement, where the model generates its own training data and you verify it with the environment, is really powerful, and it lowers the dependence on expensive human-curated data.

A few challenges remain. Reward design is tricky. If you only reward the final outcome, credit assignment across a long chain of tool calls is hard, and the model can learn to reward-hack, finding shortcuts that technically pass the check without really solving the task. Building realistic environments to train in is also a lot of engineering work. And you have to be careful that RL doesn't erode the general capabilities you got from pretraining and SFT.

But overall I'm very bullish. I think the combination, SFT for the foundation and RL for robustness and real competence, is where a lot of the progress in agentic, tool-using models is going to come from. And importantly, a lot of this is accessible to smaller teams now, not just the big labs, because you can get meaningful gains with fairly modest compute if your data and your reward signals are good.

r001.rationale: It proposes using RL to generate successful tool-use trajectories, filtering them, and feeding them back as supervised fine-tuning data.

r002.rationale: It explicitly recommends SFT as a warm start, followed by RL with outcome-based rewards.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we've thought about a lot, because I think people tend to frame it as either/or, and in practice it's really a pipeline where each piece does a different job.

The way I'd describe it is that supervised fine-tuning is great at teaching the model the format and the basic competence. If you have a model that has never seen a tool schema before, or doesn't know what a function call looks like, you don't want to discover that through RL. That's a very expensive way to learn syntax. So SFT gets you to a point where the model reliably emits well-formed calls, picks the right tool most of the time, and understands the shape of the task. It's the bootstrapping step.

Where SFT falls apart is on the multi-step stuff. If you're doing agentic tool use, where the model calls a tool, gets a result back, reasons about it, and calls another tool, the quality of your trajectory depends on decisions that compound. And with SFT you're imitating a fixed set of trajectories, which means the model never really learns what happens when it makes a mistake and has to recover. It just learns the happy path. You also run into this problem where the data you collected came from some other model or from humans, and the distribution of situations your model actually ends up in at inference time is different, so the errors compound.

That's where RL earns its keep. Once you have a model that can produce reasonable trajectories, you can let it actually interact with the environment, get a reward based on whether the task was completed, and learn from its own experience. And the nice thing in the tool-calling setting is that rewards are often fairly verifiable. Did the API call succeed? Did the final answer match? Did the test pass? That's a much cleaner signal than something like general chat quality where you need a reward model and you worry about reward hacking.

A few practical things we've found. One is that the SFT stage really matters for RL to work at all, because if your base policy almost never succeeds, you get no signal. You need some non-trivial success rate to have anything to reinforce. Two, you can be fairly loose about the SFT data quality, because RL will clean up a lot of it, but you want diversity in the tools and task types so the model doesn't get locked into narrow behaviors. And three, there's this interesting question of whether you keep mixing SFT data in during RL, as a kind of regularizer, so the model doesn't drift and forget formats or capabilities it learned earlier. We've found that helps with stability.

I'd also say the line between the two is getting blurrier. Things like rejection sampling fine-tuning, where you generate trajectories, filter by reward, and then do SFT on the good ones, that's sort of a poor man's RL, and it works surprisingly well. And it's much easier to get running than a full online RL setup. So a lot of teams start there and only graduate to something like GRPO or PPO once they've hit the ceiling on that.

So the short answer is, SFT to teach the model what tool use looks like, RL to teach it how to actually be good at it in an environment, and the real engineering work is in building environments and reward functions that are good enough that the RL signal is meaningful.

r001.rationale: It mentions generating and reward-filtering trajectories for SFT, but does not propose using an RL-trained tool-calling model to generate that training data.

r002.rationale: It explicitly presents SFT as the bootstrapping step, then says to use RL once the model can produce reasonable trajectories.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re quite complementary. Supervised fine-tuning gives you a good starting point: the model learns what a tool call looks like, which tool to select, and how to structure the arguments. Reinforcement learning can then help optimize whether those calls actually accomplish the task.

That distinction matters because there may be several valid ways to solve a problem. With supervised learning, you’re typically teaching the model to imitate a particular trajectory. With reinforcement learning, you can reward a successful outcome even if the model takes a different path. That opens up possibilities for learning when to call a tool, when to ask for clarification, and how to recover when a tool returns an error.

The challenge is defining the reward and building an environment where success is measurable. A syntactically correct call isn’t necessarily a useful call. You also want to account for things like unnecessary calls and latency, without discouraging the model from checking its work. So I’d see supervised fine-tuning as establishing the foundation, and reinforcement learning as improving the decisions the model makes on top of that.

r001.rationale: The response describes reinforcement learning improving a supervised-fine-tuned model, but does not propose using an RL-trained model to generate data for supervised fine-tuning.

r002.rationale: It explicitly presents supervised fine-tuning as the foundation, followed by reinforcement learning to improve tool-calling decisions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re very complementary. Supervised fine-tuning gives you a starting point: examples of when to call a tool, which tool to choose, and how to structure the arguments. Reinforcement learning can then help optimize whether those calls actually lead to a successful outcome.

That becomes particularly interesting when you have multiple steps. A tool call might be perfectly valid, but unnecessary, or it might return something that requires the model to change its approach. You want to reward the model for completing the task, rather than simply reproducing a particular sequence of calls.

The challenge is defining that reward. Can you verify that the task was completed? Can you account for the cost and latency of the calls? If you can build a reliable feedback loop around those things, you have a useful combination: supervised learning to establish the behavior, and reinforcement learning to improve the decisions the model makes as it interacts with tools.

r001.rationale: The response says supervised fine-tuning establishes tool-calling behavior and reinforcement learning improves it; it does not propose using an RL-trained model to generate supervised training data.

r002.rationale: It explicitly describes supervised fine-tuning as the starting point, followed by reinforcement learning to optimize tool-use decisions.
